title: Coastal mean sea level gave no clear monthly tidal-range reconstruction gain in two US bays in 2011-2025
abstract: We tested whether same-month coastal mean sea level improves monthly inland-minus-mouth tidal-range reconstruction in Delaware and Chesapeake bays. We used four fixed NOAA gauge snapshots and 407 matched months in 1991-2025. Expanding fits used prior calendar years to reconstruct 179 months in 2011-2025. Controls were month effects, a linear trend and an 18.61-year cycle. Adding coastal mean sea level reduced the equal-bay mean squared error by 0.56%. The conditional 95% three-year block interval was -3.24% to 4.56%. Bay gains were -0.17% in Delaware and 3.49% in Chesapeake; both intervals included zero. A full-record Chesapeake partial slope was negative, but neither bay had a clear late-minus-early slope change. Planned range, cycle and inferred-value checks gave no clear score gain. This is a concurrent reconstruction test, not a forecast or a physical depth-response estimate. Four gauges, short dependent records, final data snapshots, unmeasured forcing and conditional uncertainty limit inference. Code, provenance, annual error sums, all uncertainty draws, numerical checks and a figure are included.

display.caption: Annual reconstruction gains and conditional three-year block intervals. Zero means equal mean squared error. Same-month coastal mean sea level is an observed input.
